title: The bluff of the century
event: 2003 WSOP Main Event — heads-up, Chris Moneymaker against Sam Farha
blurb: An amateur who qualified online against one of the most feared pros in the game, heads-up for the world title. Play either seat.
facts: Blinds 20,000/40,000 with a 5,000 ante. Heads-up, so Moneymaker's button is also the small blind and he acts first before the flop, last after it.
Stacks are about 5.7 million (Moneymaker) and 2.7 million (Farha): CardPlayer gives the counts after this hand, 6.6 million and 1.8 million, and the chips Farha put in are added back.
ending: Farha thought for a long time — by his own account about twenty minutes, most of which the broadcast did not show — and folded his pair of nines. Moneymaker had king-high. The pot moved him to about 6.6 million against 1.8 million, and the tournament ended on the very next hand.

1.intro: You are Sam Farha, a top professional, heads-up for the world championship against an amateur. You hold Q♠ 9♥ in the big blind.

1.ask: Moneymaker raises to 100,000 from the button. You hold Q♠ 9♥. What do you do?

notes.fold: Too tight heads-up. With only one opponent, a hand like queen-nine is well above average, and you are getting a good price to see a flop.
notes.call: What Farha did. A cheap call keeps the pot small with a decent but not premium hand.
notes.raise: Reasonable too — heads-up, queen-nine is often the best hand. It builds a bigger pot with a hand that does not love one.

1.why: Heads-up, almost any hand with a queen is worth seeing a flop for at this price. Farha called rather than re-raising, keeping the pot manageable.
1.lesson: Heads-up, hands go up in value: there is only one other hand to beat, so a queen-nine you would fold at a full table is a call here.

2.ask: The flop is 9♠ 2♦ 6♠. You have top pair — nines with a queen kicker. You act first. Check or bet?

notes.check: What Farha did. Checking can trap a player who will bet a worse hand, but it also lets a drawing hand see the next card for free.
notes.bet: Charges the draws — two spades are out — while you are ahead. Top pair is a hand that likes the pot to grow a little.

2.why: Moneymaker, by his own account, read the check as a plan to check and call with top pair rather than build a big pot against him. Both players checked, and the turn came free.
2.lesson: A free card is not free for you: the player with the draw gets to try again without paying. Top pair on a board with a flush draw usually wants to make draws pay.

4.ask: The turn is the 8♠ — now three spades and four cards near a straight. You still have top pair. You act first. Check or bet?

notes.check: Keeps the pot small on a board that just got scary for a single pair.
notes.bet: What Farha did — 300,000 into a 210,000 pot. A large bet that represents strength but builds a big pot with only one pair.

4.why: Farha led out big. PokerNews's analysis argues he "really shouldn't be leading" after checking the flop — a one-pair hand on a board like this would rather keep the pot under control.
4.lesson: When the board gets more dangerous, one pair gets weaker. Betting big into it invites exactly the raise you do not want to face.

6.ask: Moneymaker raises to 800,000. Top pair on a board with three spades and a possible straight. Call, fold, or move all in?

notes.fold: Gives up a lot of chips with top pair against a player who could be raising a draw.
notes.call: What Farha did. Keeps his options open for the river, at a high price.
notes.allin: Ends the hand now and denies the draws their river card — but against a flush or a straight you are close to drawing dead.
notes.raise: A re-raise short of all in commits a lot of chips with one pair on a board that has just got dangerous — and leaves you facing an all-in you may not want to call.

6.why: Farha called and waited for the river. The raise could mean a made flush or straight — or a big draw.
6.lesson: A raise on a scary board narrows the other player's hand to two kinds: very strong, or a draw. A single pair beats only the draws.

7.ask: The river is the 3♥ — a blank. The flush and the straight did not get there. You act first. Check or bet?

notes.check: What Farha did. Lets a missed draw bluff — and gets you to a decision you may not want.
notes.bet: Gets value from a worse pair and takes the bluff away. But a flush or straight made on the turn would raise you.

7.why: Farha checked, which handed the initiative back to Moneymaker.
7.lesson: Checking the river gives a player who missed one last chance to bluff. Sometimes that is the plan; know that it is.

9.ask: Moneymaker moves all in — you would have to put in all your remaining chips, about 1.8 million. Call or fold?

notes.fold: What Farha did. He laid down the best hand.
notes.call: Would have won the pot and the chip lead — with hindsight. At the time, it risked his tournament against a range full of flushes and straights.

9.why: PokerNews's analysis does not call the fold a mistake: an all-in here tells you he holds a straight or better, or nothing at all — and against that, one pair is only a bluff catcher. Farha said afterwards that he talked himself out of the call.
9.lesson: A bluff catcher can only beat a bluff. The question is not "is my hand good?" but "how often is this a bluff?" — and you will sometimes fold the winner. That is part of the game, not proof the fold was wrong.

0.intro: You are Chris Moneymaker, an accountant who won his seat online, heads-up for the world championship against Sam Farha. You hold K♠ 7♥ on the button.

0.ask: You are on the button with K♠ 7♥. You act first. Fold, limp, or raise?

notes.fold: Too tight. Heads-up, king-seven is well above average.
notes.call: Plays a smaller pot, but gives up the chance to win the blinds right away.
notes.raise: What Moneymaker did. Heads-up, raising most hands from the button is standard.

0.why: Heads-up, the button raises a wide range: there is only one player to get past, and you act last after the flop.
0.lesson: Heads-up, raise a lot from the button. A king with any kicker is a strong hand when there is only one opponent.

3.ask: The flop is 9♠ 2♦ 6♠ and Farha checks. You have king-high with the K♠ — one spade. Check or bet?

notes.check: What Moneymaker did. Takes a free card with king-high and a backdoor flush draw.
notes.bet: A continuation bet often wins the pot right away — but a player who checks top pair here is not going anywhere.

3.why: Moneymaker checked behind and took the free card.
3.lesson: When you check behind, you see the next card for free — useful with a hand that can improve.

5.ask: The turn is the 8♠. You now have a flush draw (four spades with the king) and an open-ended straight draw (a 5 or a 10). Farha bets 300,000. Fold, call, or raise?

notes.fold: Throws away a big draw with many outs.
notes.call: Sees the river at a fair price for a draw this strong.
notes.raise: What Moneymaker did — a semi-bluff. It can win the pot now, and it can still make the best hand on the river.

5.why: A raise with a big draw is called a semi-bluff: if Farha folds you win now, and if he calls you still have outs. PokerNews notes this line differs from what players would usually choose today.
5.lesson: Semi-bluff with strong draws: you win if they fold, and you can still win if they call and you hit.

8.ask: The river is the 3♥. You missed everything — king-high. Farha checks. Check, or move all in?

notes.check: Your king-high almost never wins a showdown. Checking means you have lost the hand.
notes.allin: What Moneymaker did. The only way to win: make Farha fold a better hand.
notes.bet: A smaller bluff risks less, but against top pair it rarely gets a fold — the threat of losing everything is what made Farha think so long.

8.why: PokerNews describes the all-in as telegraphing a "polarized" range: a straight or better, or nothing. Moneymaker had nothing — and that is exactly why it could work. His story on the turn (the raise) matched a made hand.
8.lesson: A bluff only works when the story makes sense. Your bets on earlier streets must match the strong hand you are pretending to have.

sources.what: Cards, suits, board, every bet, blinds and ante, and the turn pot of 210,000
sources.by: PokerNews — Analyzing Moneymaker's 'Bluff of the Century' Against Farha

sources.what: Every bet amount confirmed, and the chip counts after the hand (6.6 million and 1.8 million)
K-7 against Q-9, a 9-6-2 flop with two spades, the eight of spades giving Moneymaker a flush draw and an open-ended straight draw, the river all-in; Farha's own account of the fold
sources.by: Grantland — When We Held Kings (oral history)

sources.what: King-high bluff, Farha folds a pair of nines
Three spades on the board, king-high, Farha's top pair of nines

conflicts: CardPlayer gives the hand as K♦7♦ against Q♠9♠ on 9♠6♦2♠ 8♠ 3♠. That cannot be right: it puts the 9♠ in Farha's hand and on the flop, and four spades on the board. PokerNews's suits have no duplicates and match Grantland's account — two spades on the flop, the 8♠ giving Moneymaker a flush draw — so they are used here.

PokerNews says the players began heads-up with 4.6 million and 3.7 million. Those are the counts at the start of heads-up play, not at this hand: they do not add up with CardPlayer's counts after it. The stacks here are worked back from CardPlayer's after-hand counts.
